desc:
Find the greatest length L such that some substring of s of length L and some substring of t of the same length L differ in at most k positions (compare them character by character at the same offsets).

Return L; it is 0 when no length works (for instance if a string is empty).

s = "abcdef", t = "abxdyf", k = 1  ->  4   ("abcd" vs "abxd")
s = "abcdef", t = "abxdyf", k = 2  ->  6
s = "aaaa",   t = "bbbb",   k = 2  ->  2
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: With k = 0 this is the longest common substring. The key observation there is that a pair of substrings is described by their start positions, and the next pair of characters always lies on the same diagonal i - j.
Fix the diagonal d = i - j. Along it you compare s[i] with t[i - d] and get a sequence of match/mismatch flags. The task on one diagonal is: the longest window with at most k mismatches.

Use a sliding window on every diagonal: extend the right end, count mismatches, and move the left end forward while the count exceeds k. Take the best window over all diagonals. There are m + n - 1 diagonals with a total of m · n cells.
editorial: Two equal-length substrings starting at s[i] and t[j] are compared character by character, so the pairs (s[i+x], t[j+x]) all lie on the diagonal with offset i - j. Every candidate pair of substrings therefore corresponds to a contiguous window along one diagonal of the m by n grid whose cell (i, j) is a mismatch when s[i] != t[j].

The answer is the longest window, over all diagonals, that contains at most k mismatching cells. On a single diagonal this is the classic 'longest window with at most k bad elements' problem solved with two pointers in linear time: advance the right end, add one to the counter if the new cell is a mismatch, and while the counter exceeds k advance the left end (subtracting if the cell it leaves was a mismatch). The window never shrinks below a valid state and each pointer moves at most the diagonal length.
In total the work is the number of grid cells, O(m · n). The naive approach of trying every pair of start positions and every length is O(m · n · min(m, n)) or worse.
